t: Armenian is a branch of the Indo-European family on its own; in 1875 Heinrich Hübschmann showed that it is not an Iranian language, despite its many Parthian and Persian loanwords.
Written since Mesrop Mashtots created its alphabet in 405, it kept Classical Armenian, or Grabar, as its literary standard from the 5th century to the 19th.
Two modern standards grew up in the 19th century: Eastern Armenian, the official language of Armenia, and Western Armenian, carried by the diaspora after the Armenian genocide.
dyk: Because Armenian borrowed so much, only around 1,500 words of Classical Armenian are known to have been inherited from Indo-European; even its word for “skull”, xalam, is thought to come from an Anatolian language, cognate with Hittite ḫalanta, “head”.
ev: Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet of 36 letters
The Bible is translated into Armenian, the language’s oldest surviving text
Gregory of Narek writes the Book of Lamentations, adding well above a thousand new words to the literary language
In Bagratid Armenia and the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia the letters օ and ֆ are added to the alphabet
Azdarar, the first Armenian periodical, is published in Classical Armenian
Heinrich Hübschmann uses the comparative method to show that Armenian is not an Iranian language
A spelling reform in Soviet Armenia adds the letter և and makes ու a single letter

f.family: Indo-European; the sole member of an independent Armenian branch, often thought closest to Greek (the Graeco-Armenian hypothesis), though whether through common descent or long contact is debated
f.script: the Armenian alphabet, created by Mesrop Mashtots in 405 with 36 letters; օ and ֆ added in the Middle Ages (38 letters); a reformed spelling with the new letter և in Soviet Armenia in the 1920s, while the diaspora keeps the traditional alphabet and spelling
f.earliest: a 5th-century translation of the Bible, its oldest surviving text, and the Armenian Alexander Romance, also translated in the 5th century; the Armenians themselves are named in the 6th-century BC Behistun Inscription and in Xenophon’s Anabasis
f.status: living: between five and seven million speakers worldwide (Ethnologue: 3.7 million Eastern and 1.6 million Western Armenian speakers, 5.3 million in all); the official language of Armenia, a recognised minority language in Cyprus, Hungary, Iraq, Poland and Romania, and protected in Turkey by the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne
